paras: The lynching of Alonzo Holly took place at Pinckneyville, Perry County, Illinois, early on February 14, 1888, when masked men took Holly, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from a tree nearby. Holly was held on a charge of assaulting a white woman near St. Johns. A Pinckneyville correspondent called it "the first lynching that ever occurred in Perry county," and wire dispatches carried it nationwide within a day.

Holly, called "a negro" and "colored" in the dispatches, was accused of assaulting a white woman, described in the Duquoin and Belleville reports as a coal miner's wife. Accounts placed the alleged assault at St. Johns or Duquoin and dated it from November to five weeks before the lynching, and the New York Sun described it in detail as fact, with nothing from Holly's side. A mob had earlier come from St. Johns to lynch him, but officers took him to Belleville, where he became "so troublesome" that officials sent him back to Pinckneyville the Saturday before his death.

At about 2 a.m. men knocked at the jail, where Sheriff Penwarden ("Renwarden" in one account) boarded with the jailer, Jeff King. The sheriff argued with them from a window until he was "promptly covered with shotguns," and six men with two shotguns and four revolvers got in and took the keys to the cells. The Post-Dispatch wire said instead that the sheriff first refused and then admitted the men when they made ready to batter the doors.

The men bound Holly and put a rope around his neck; he begged for two minutes to pray and, refused, asked a fellow prisoner, John Eaton, to pray for him. At the door he pulled back, was jerked onto his face and dragged about fifty feet to a maple tree, and was hanged from a limb about eight feet up. The Duquoin dispatch added that Holly "protested his innocence to the last." The sheriff and jailer found him dead a few feet from the jail after the men dispersed, unseen, in different directions.

An inquest the same day returned a verdict of "hanging by unknown parties," and the Sun reported that "The vigilantes are not known." No report of arrests, grand jury action or the trial of John Eaton appears in the coverage. A December 1888 list of "Victims of Judge Lynch" entered Holly under February 14.

The story broke on February 15 through three separate dispatches: a Pinckneyville special in the New York Sun, a St. Louis Post-Dispatch special, and a Duquoin special to the St. Louis Chronicle. The Post-Dispatch version ran that day in the Savannah Morning News, the Memphis Appeal, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Omaha Daily Bee, and the Atlanta Constitution printed its own long Pinckneyville special, which called it the first lynching in Perry County, on February 21. Weeklies from Montana to North Dakota and Wisconsin, as well as the Western Appeal of St. Paul, cut it to a line saying a mob lynched Holly "for criminally assaulting a white woman."

Headlines treated the accusation as proven: "Sixty Men Force a Sheriff to Surrender a Ravisher" in the Savannah Morning News, "A Negro Lynched for the Usual Crime" in the Newberry Herald and News, and "Met with Summary Justice" in the Beatrice Daily Express. The Sun called the alleged crime "particularly brutal," and the Atlanta correspondent called Holly "a bad negro generally" who left "a white wife about twice his own age." Only the Duquoin dispatch reported anything said in Holly's defense.

Southern papers also turned the case against the North. The Savannah Morning News reprinted a Chicago News remark that "An Illinois mob lynched a negro the other day" while Senator Sherman and other "emotional statesmen" pointed "accusing fingers at the solid South."

The Sun put the whole mob at "about fifty men," the Post-Dispatch wire at sixty, and the Chronicle and Belleville dispatches at twenty, while the Atlanta account mentioned only the six who entered the jail. The hour ranged from 2 a.m. to 4 a.m., and the Belleville dispatch had Holly dragged "through the streets to a grove" rather than fifty feet to a tree.

accounts.label: Pinckneyville special (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: Six masked men from St. John's, part of a mob of about fifty, forced the sheriff to surrender the keys at gunpoint, dragged Holly fifty feet and hanged him from a maple; 'The vigilantes are not known.'

accounts.label: Pinckneyville special (Atlanta Constitution)
accounts.gist: Fullest version: jailer opened the door to save it, six armed men took the keys, Holly hanged from a maple limb; inquest found 'hanging by unknown parties.'

accounts.label: St. Louis Post-Dispatch wire
accounts.gist: A mob of sixty marched from St. Johns; the sheriff refused, then admitted them when they prepared to batter the door; Holly hanged fifty yards from the jail.

accounts.label: St. Louis Chronicle, Duquoin special
accounts.gist: Twenty masked men hanged Holly about 3:30 a.m. in a residential street; the alleged victim was a coal miner's wife assaulted five weeks earlier; Holly protested his innocence.

accounts.label: Belleville dispatch
accounts.gist: Twenty masked men broke open the jail at 4 a.m. and dragged Holly to a grove; the alleged assault was in November.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Sixty Men Force a Sheriff to Surrender a Ravisher', 'A Negro Lynched for the Usual Crime', 'A Ravisher Lynched', 'Met with Summary Justice' treat the charge as proven.
The Sun and Atlanta specials narrate the victim's pleading and the mob's force in detail while calling the crime 'particularly brutal' and Holly 'a bad negro generally.'
Digest briefs repeat that a mob lynched Holly 'for criminally assaulting a white woman.'
Savannah Morning News reprints a Chicago News quip using the Illinois lynching to rebut Northern criticism of the 'solid South.'
